headline: Support Group for People Who Accidentally Liked Old Posts While Stalking Reaches 500,000 Members
subheadline: Community processes the specific horror of the 2 AM deep-scroll incident
summary: A Threadit community for those who have accidentally revealed their social media stalking has become a massive support network.
content:
The Threadit community r/AccidentalArchaeologists has reached 500,000 members, all united by a shared trauma: accidentally liking someone's post from years ago while deep-scrolling their profile at an inappropriate hour.

"It was 2:47 AM," recounted user @ScrolledTooFar. "I was 847 posts deep on my ex's new girlfriend's cousin's InstaSnap. My thumb slipped. I liked a beach photo from 2019. I saw my own username appear. I threw my phone across the room. It didn't help. The like was already out there."

The community has developed a taxonomy of incidents. "The Ex Deep-Dive" involves romantic interests. "The Crush Reconnaissance" covers potential partners. "The Professional Spiral" describes accidentally liking a coworker's vacation photos from before you worked together. All are treated with equal gravity.

"There's no recovering from a 3 AM like on a four-year-old photo," wrote moderator @DigitalForensicVictim. "You can unlike it, but they already got the notification. They know. They know you were looking. The only question is: do they care enough to judge you?"

Support strategies shared on the forum range from technical ("turn off double-tap to like") to philosophical ("everyone stalks, we just got caught"). The most upvoted advice: "Own it. Like five more posts. Establish dominance."

The community processes incidents in real-time. A recent post titled "I just liked my boss's wedding photo from 2016 what do I do" received 847 responses within an hour, ranging from "move to a new city" to "pretend you were hacked."

"I told my crush I was 'cleaning up old likes for privacy reasons,'" shared @LamestExcuse. "She asked why I was cleaning up likes on her profile. I pretended my phone died."

Psychologist Dr. Nina Patel called the community "a perfect example of how shared embarrassment builds connection. These people found each other because they all made the same mistake. There's comfort in that."

The community's banner reads: "No judgment. Only understanding. Your secret's safe with 499,999 strangers."
author: Sandra Kim, Community Correspondent
